(1) the extreme summer drought of 2012 induced species-specific die back in woody species of Northeastern Italy; (2) Prunus mahaleb, a species with deep roots, maintained higher water potential, gas exchange and non-structural carbon content throughout the summer, while Quercus pubesccens and Ostry carpinifolia showed a significant hydraulic failure; (3) our data support the hypothesis drought-induced tree decline cannot be modelled based on single predictors

(i) an extreme summer drought in northeastern Italy induced species-specific die back; (ii) the drought-induced die back was associated with a significant loss of stem hydraulic conductivity in the most impacted species, Quercus pubesens and Ostry carpinifolia; (iii) the drought-resistant Prunus mahalab was characterized by a deep root system, which allowed the tree to maintain high water potential and non-structural carbon content throughout the summer.
the species-specific response to an extreme drought in 2012 was associated with differences in rooting depth, water relations, gas exchange and non-structural carbon dynamics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of water availability in the maintenance of tree hydraulic status.

the role of water and carbon balance in the seasonal progression of drought-related hydraulic failure in woody species, and with the possible role of rooting depth as a predictor of species-specific drought response.

the identification of traits that can help to explain species-specific responses to extreme drought events, and can contribute to the development of predictive models for the management of forest ecosystems in the face of global change.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the extreme summer drought of 2012 in Northeastern Italy induced die-back in Quercus and Ostrya, but not in Prunus, due to differences in rooting depth.

the drought-induced tree die-back is a complex phenomenon, and that a single predictor of tree status, such as hydraulic efficiency, vulnerability, carbohydrate content and root system depth, cannot be used to predict tree decline.
drought-induced die-back is not simply a hydraulic phenomenon, but a multi-factorial phenomenon involving water and carbon dynamics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
species with deeper roots can maintain higher water potential, gas exchange rates and NSC, and relatively stable maintenance of hydraulic conductivity (k), even during extreme droughts.
the ability to maintain water relations and NSC is the key to the ability to maintain vascular integrity, which in turn is the key to survival of woody plants during extreme drought.
the ability to maintain water and energy balance in extreme drought conditions is related to the capacity to maintain the hydraulic system intact.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the drought response of woody species cannot be reduced to a single mechanism, but it is the result of a complex interaction between several physiological and morphological traits.
a deeper rooting system is a key trait to maintain a favourable water status during drought, which is crucial for tree survival.
the role of root depth in tree water relations and drought resistance has been underestimated.
